items.q: The council ____ a resolution condemning the coup.
items.e: „to adopt a resolution“ — VN-Terminus.

items.q: The deal was struck after ____ bargaining.
items.e: „hard bargaining“ = zähes Feilschen; „heavy“ wäre die deutsche Interferenz.

items.q: The two positions are ____ irreconcilable.
items.e: „irreconcilable" ist ein absolutes Adjektiv und verträgt nur verstärkende Adverbien: „fundamentally irreconcilable". Ausgeschlossen sind: „marginally" und „partially" (beide graduieren, was keinen Grad kennt — etwas ist entweder unvereinbar oder nicht); „nominally" (nur dem Namen nach — es hieße, die Unvereinbarkeit bestehe gar nicht).

items.q: The measure was adopted ____ a large majority.
items.e: „adopted by a majority“ — feste Präposition.

items.q: a ____ of protest from member states
items.e: „a chorus of protest/criticism“ — feste Kollokation.

items.q: The negotiations ____ down over subsidies.
items.e: „to bog down“ = ins Stocken geraten.

items.q: The chair sought to ____ over the divisions.
items.e: „to smooth over differences" ist das feste Phrasal Verb für das Glätten von Gegensätzen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „soothe" (beruhigen — transitiv, ohne „over"); „soften" („soften up" gibt es, „soften over" nicht); „sweeten" („sweeten the deal" ist die Fügung, „sweeten over" existiert nicht).

items.q: The clause was ____ from the final text.
items.e: „to expunge“ = tilgen/streichen.

items.q: The parties agreed to a ____ ceasefire.
items.e: „provisional ceasefire“ = vorläufig; „providential“ = glücklich fügend.

items.q: It was a ____ point of order, not a real objection.
items.e: „a mere point of order“ = bloß; die Nuance trennt „mere/sheer/bare“.

items.q: The ambassador ____ a toast to the host.
items.e: „to propose a toast" ist die feste Wendung des gesellschaftlichen Protokolls. Ausgeschlossen sind: „pledged" (etwas zusagen oder geloben — man gelobt keinen Trinkspruch); „declared" (etwas förmlich erklären, von Ergebnissen und Zuständen); „announced" (ankündigen — der Trinkspruch wird ausgebracht, nicht angekündigt).

items.q: The reform is dead in the ____ .
items.e: Idiom: „dead in the water“ = aussichtslos festgefahren.

items.q: The minister denied any involvement in any way, shape or ____ .
items.e: Die feste Dreierformel lautet „in any way, shape or form" (= in keinerlei Hinsicht). Die anderen Wörter sind zwar Synonyme von „Art", stehen in dieser Wendung aber nicht.

items.q: The appointment was made ex ____ .
items.e: Latinismus: „ex officio“ = von Amts wegen.

items.q: The evidence was ruled ____ .
items.e: „to rule evidence inadmissible" ist die feste Wendung des Prozessrechts: das Beweismittel wird nicht zugelassen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „admissible" (das Gegenteil: zulässig); „indispensable" (unentbehrlich — ein Werturteil über die Bedeutung, keine Zulassungsentscheidung); „indefensible" (nicht zu rechtfertigen, von Verhalten und Positionen).

items.q: The court noted the ____ of the two accounts.
items.e: „the divergence of two accounts" bezeichnet deren Auseinandergehen — Abweichungen zwischen zwei Darstellungen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „diversion" (Ablenkung bzw. Umleitung); „diversity" (Vielfalt, die eine Mehrzahl voraussetzt); „division" (Teilung oder Spaltung, nicht das Abweichen zweier Aussagen voneinander).

items.q: The plan is still at a ____ stage.
items.e: „a preliminary stage“ = Vorstufe; „premature“ = verfrüht.

items.q: A British 'lift' is an American ____ .
items.e: BE „lift“ = AE „elevator“.

items.q: Sources described the mood as 'cautious' — meaning ____ .
items.e: Diplomatensprache: „cautious“ signalisiert gedämpfte Erwartungen.

items.q: Calls for his resignation are ____ louder.
items.e: „growing louder“ — feste Kollokation für zunehmende Lautstärke/Intensität; „raising“ ist transitiv und verlangt ein Objekt, funktioniert hier allein nicht.

items.q: The minister was ____ aware of the precedent.
items.e: „painfully aware“ — feste Intensivierer-Kollokation.

items.q: „Streitbeilegung“ (WTO) — das exakte englische Äquivalent:
items.e: WTO-Terminus: „dispute settlement“.

items.q: „Zollunion“ — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: Handelsterminus: „customs union“.

items.q: „Vergeltungsmaßnahmen“ (Handel) — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: „retaliatory measures“; völkerrechtlich auch „countermeasures“.

items.q: „Subventionen“ — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: Handelsterminus: „subsidies“.

items.q: „Präambel“ (eines Vertrags) — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: Vertragsterminus: „preamble“; die anderen gehören zu Büchern.

items.q: It was the second time that session the vote ____ without explanation.
items.e: Nach „it was the second time" steht zwingend das Past Perfect: „had been postponed". Ausgeschlossen sind: „was postponed" (Präteritum, das der Rahmen nicht zulässt); „has been postponed" (gehörte zu „it is the second time"); „would be postponed" (Zukunft in der Vergangenheit).

items.q: Not one of the pledges ____ honoured by the time the review conference opened.
items.e: „by the time" + Vergangenheit verlangt Vorzeitigkeit, also das Past Perfect Passiv „had been honoured". Ausgeschlossen sind: „was" und „were" (Präteritum drückt keine Vorzeitigkeit aus; „were" verstößt zusätzlich gegen die Kongruenz mit „Not one", das den Singular verlangt); „have been" (Present Perfect bindet an die Gegenwart).

items.q: The ruling is binding ____ all parties.
items.e: „binding on“ — feste Fügung.

items.q: The outcome is contingent ____ ratification.
items.e: „contingent on/upon“ = abhängig von.

items.q: There was no objection ____ the proposal.
items.e: „objection to“ — Nomen-Rektion.

items.q: If the mechanism ____ revived tomorrow, disputes could once again be settled — but nobody expects that to happen.
items.e: „If X were …" ist der Irrealis; der Nachsatz „nobody expects that to happen" schließt die reale Bedingung ausdrücklich aus. Ausgeschlossen sind: „would be" (kein „would" im Bedingungssatz); „had been" (Vorzeitigkeit, unvereinbar mit „tomorrow"); „is" (realer Bedingungssatz — den der Nachsatz gerade ausschließt).

items.q: Had the panel ruled otherwise, chaos ____ .
items.e: Konditional III.

items.q: ____ the appeal succeed, the tariff would be struck down.
items.e: Invertierter Konditional Typ I.

items.q: Rarely ____ so united a front.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach „Rarely“ + Past Perfect.

items.q: The statute stipulates that the panel ____ within thirty days.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „stipulate that“.

items.q: He addressed the court as if the ruling ____ set aside by the time the hearing opened.
items.e: „by the time" + Vergangenheitspunkt markiert Vorzeitigkeit zu einem bereits vergangenen Bezugspunkt und verlangt das Past Perfect Passiv: „had been set aside". Ausgeschlossen sind: „was" (Präteritum kann keine Vorzeitigkeit zu einem anderen Vergangenheitspunkt ausdrücken — „was set aside by the time the hearing opened" ist ungrammatisch); „has been" (Present Perfect bindet an die Gegenwart und verträgt sich nicht mit dem abgeschlossenen Zeitrahmen „by the time the hearing opened"); „were" (Konjunktiv Präsens nach „as if" beschreibt eine gegenwärtige Irrealität und kollidiert überdies im Numerus mit „the ruling").

items.q: The bloc risks ____ its own principles.
items.e: „risk“ + Gerundium.

items.q: They went on ____ the treaty despite the warnings.
items.e: „go on to do“ = danach etwas Neues tun.

items.q: The mechanism ____ to have been paralysed for years.
items.e: Berichtspassiv: „is said to have been“.

items.q: The lights were off; the office ____ have been empty.
items.e: Epistemisches „must have been“.

items.q: Five judges dissented, two of ____ wrote separately.
items.e: „two of whom“ — Personenbezug nach Präposition.

items.q: ____ properly enforced, the rule would deter defection.
items.e: Invertierter Konditional II.

items.q: It is the fourth time the panel ____ deadlocked.
items.e: „the fourth time … “ + Present Perfect.

items.q: By next session, the reform ____ into force.
items.e: „by next session“ + Future Perfect.

items.q: A number of proposals ____ been tabled since the recess.
items.e: „a number of …" ist eine Mengenangabe; das Bezugswort ist der Plural „proposals", das Prädikat steht deshalb im Plural: „have been tabled". Ausgeschlossen sind: „has" (Singular — der gälte nur für „the number of"); „are" und „were" (Formen von „be", die vor dem Partizip „been" nicht stehen können).

items.q: Not until the ruling did the members ____ the full cost.
items.e: Nach der Inversion („did … members“) folgt der bloße Infinitiv „grasp“.

items.q: The compromise is ____ elegant as it is fragile.
items.e: Vergleich „as … as“.

items.q: ____ its flaws, the system still functions.
items.e: „For all its flaws“ = trotz; konzessive Nominalphrase.

items.q: It was the enforcement, ____ the rules, that failed.
items.e: Kontrast in der Cleft: „It was the enforcement, not the rules, that …“.

items.q: The bloc must not do ____ with the appellate stage.
items.e: „do away with“ = abschaffen.

items.q: By then the deadlock ____ for the better part of two years.
items.e: „By then" verweist auf einen Punkt der Vergangenheit und verlangt für das bereits Andauernde das Past Perfect. Ausgeschlossen sind: „persisted" (Präteritum ohne Vorzeitigkeit); „would persist" (Zukunft in der Vergangenheit); „has persisted" (Present Perfect mit Gegenwartsbezug, unvereinbar mit „by then").

items.q: The word 'liturgy' applied to climate summits suggests they have become …
o: an efficient machine for taking binding decisions.
a repetitive ritual observed regardless of results.
a sacred duty that stands beyond all criticism.
a purely scientific undertaking without politics.
items.e: „Liturgie“: eingespieltes Ritual, jährlich gleich — unabhängig vom Ertrag.
items.passage:
Climate summits have perfected a peculiar liturgy. Each year the faithful gather; each year the final text is wrenched from deadlock in the small hours; each year a weary chair gavels through language hailed as historic and denounced, within the hour, as hollow. The ritual is easy to mock, and mockery is largely deserved. Yet to conclude that the process is therefore worthless is to misread what it is for. Summits do not, by themselves, cut a single tonne of carbon; what they do is convert diffuse pressure into dated commitments against which laggards can later be measured and shamed.

The trouble is that shame is a currency of diminishing value in a world where the largest emitters have grown indifferent to it, and where the departure of one great power from the central treaty has licensed others to lower their gaze. The optimistic reading holds that implementation has quietly overtaken negotiation — that while diplomats haggle over adjectives, engineers and financiers are decarbonising faster than any communiqué requires. There is truth in this, but also a hazard: if the summits become mere theatre, the pressure they once concentrated will dissipate, and the implementers will lose the political cover that ambition at the top once gave them. The gathering matters less for what it decides than for what it signals about whether the world still intends to try.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: The author concedes that 'mockery is largely deserved' but insists this ____ .
o: does not make the process worthless.
items.e: Konzession mit Einschränkung: Spott berechtigt, doch daraus folgt keine Wertlosigkeit.

The gathering matters less for what it decides than for what it signals about whether the world still intends to try.

items.q: The 'hazard' the author identifies in that optimistic reading is that …
o: engineers will decarbonise faster than governments can legislate.
diplomats will abandon the haggling over adjectives and go home early.
implementation will be rendered illegal under the central treaty.
if summits become theatre, the pressure implementers rely on dissipates.
items.e: Gefahr: Wird der Gipfel zum Theater, entfällt der politische Deckungsschutz für die Umsetzer.
items.passage:
Climate summits have perfected a peculiar liturgy. Each year the faithful gather; each year the final text is wrenched from deadlock in the small hours; each year a weary chair gavels through language hailed as historic and denounced, within the hour, as hollow. The ritual is easy to mock, and mockery is largely deserved. Yet to conclude that the process is therefore worthless is to misread what it is for. Summits do not, by themselves, cut a single tonne of carbon; what they do is convert diffuse pressure into dated commitments against which laggards can later be measured and shamed.

The trouble is that shame is a currency of diminishing value in a world where the largest emitters have grown indifferent to it, and where the departure of one great power from the central treaty has licensed others to lower their gaze. The optimistic reading holds that implementation has quietly overtaken negotiation — that while diplomats haggle over adjectives, engineers and financiers are decarbonising faster than any communiqué requires. There is truth in this, but also a hazard: if the summits become mere theatre, the pressure they once concentrated will dissipate, and the implementers will lose the political cover that ambition at the top once gave them. The gathering matters less for what it decides than for what it signals about whether the world still intends to try.

items.q: The final sentence locates the summits' true value in what they ____ .
o: decide about specific national emission targets.
spend on the logistics of the conference itself.
signal about the world's continued intent to try.
prohibit outright under binding international law.
items.e: Schlusspointe: Bedeutung liegt im Signal des Weiter-Wollens, nicht in einzelnen Beschlüssen.

items.q: The pledge ____ short of a binding target.
items.e: „to fall short of“ = zurückbleiben hinter.

items.q: Negotiators faced a ____ deadline.
items.e: „a looming deadline“ = drohend nahende Frist.

items.q: The text was ____ watered down overnight.
items.e: „heavily watered down“ — feste Kollokation.

items.q: The commitment takes effect ____ 2030, superseding all prior arrangements.
items.e: „as of 2030“ = mit Wirkung ab 2030; „by“ würde einen Termin VOR dem alle Vereinbarungen abgelöst werden implizieren, nicht den Startpunkt, „since“ verlangt Vergangenheitsbezug, „at“ ist mit Jahreszahlen nicht idiomatisch.

items.q: a ____ in global temperatures
items.e: „a rise in temperatures“; „raise“ ist transitiv/Verb.

items.q: The parties agreed to ____ up their ambitions.
items.e: „to scale up" heißt, etwas im Umfang zu vergrößern. Ausgeschlossen sind: „wind up" (abschließen, beenden — das Gegenteil); „turn up" (auftauchen bzw. lauter stellen); „stack up" (sich häufen oder im Vergleich abschneiden).

items.q: The chair tried to ____ over the divisions in the plenary.
items.e: „to gloss over“ = beschönigend übergehen.

items.q: The pledge was ____ by a lack of funding.
items.e: „to undermine" heißt, etwas von unten aushöhlen und dadurch entwerten — die feste Wendung für ein durch fehlende Mittel entkräftetes Versprechen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „underlaid" (unterlegt, im wörtlichen Sinn); „understated" (untertrieben dargestellt — es ginge um die Darstellung, nicht die Wirkung); „underwritten" (finanziell abgesichert — das genaue Gegenteil).

items.q: The commitment remains ____ , not legally binding.
items.e: „aspirational“ = Absichtserklärung ohne Bindung.

items.q: It was a ____ gesture, with no real effect.
items.e: „a token gesture" ist die symbolische Geste, die nur der Form halber erfolgt. Ausgeschlossen sind: „tacit" (stillschweigend, unausgesprochen — eine Geste ist gerade sichtbar); „tepid" (lauwarm — es bewertete die Aufnahme, nicht die Geste); „tangible" (greifbar, mit realer Wirkung — das Gegenteil von „no real effect").

items.q: Delegates ____ the risk of coastal flooding.
items.e: „to flag a risk/issue“ = auf etwas hinweisen/markieren.

items.q: The pledges are a drop in the ____ .
items.e: Idiom: „a drop in the ocean“ = ein Tropfen auf den heißen Stein.

items.q: The delegates worked around the ____ .
items.e: Idiom: „around the clock“ = rund um die Uhr.

items.q: The parties agreed, mutatis mutandis, to a ____ vivendi.
items.e: Latinismus: „modus vivendi“ = tragfähiges Auskommen.

items.q: The target proved wholly ____ .
items.e: „unattainable" = nicht erreichbar; „un-" ist die etablierte Verneinung dieses Stamms. Ausgeschlossen sind: „attainable" (das Gegenteil); „unavailable" (nicht verfügbar — von Personen und Mitteln, nicht von Zielen); „unattended" (unbeaufsichtigt).

items.q: The summit's ____ was widely questioned.
items.e: „credibility" ist die Glaubwürdigkeit — das, was in Zweifel gezogen wird. Ausgeschlossen sind: „credulity" (Leichtgläubigkeit, eine Eigenschaft des Publikums, nicht des Gipfels); „credentials" (Beglaubigungsschreiben bzw. Qualifikationen, stets im Plural); „credit" (Anerkennung bzw. Kredit).

items.q: The scheme is still ____ in its scope.
items.e: „modest in scope“ = bescheiden; die anderen tragen den Mangel-Ton.

items.q: A British 'tap' is an American ____ .
items.e: BE „tap“ = AE „faucet“.

items.q: Officials called the outcome 'a step in the right direction' — meaning ____ .
items.e: Diplomatenformel: signalisiert bescheidenen, unzureichenden Fortschritt.

items.q: Concern over the shortfall is ____ by the day.
items.e: „deepening concern“ = sich vertiefende Besorgnis — feste Kollokation.

items.q: The chair was ____ conscious of the stakes.
items.e: „keenly conscious“ = sich lebhaft bewusst — feste Intensivierer-Kollokation.

items.q: „Anpassungsfinanzierung“ (Klima) — das exakte englische Äquivalent:
items.e: Klimaterminus: „adaptation finance“.

items.q: „Verursacherprinzip“ — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: Umweltrechtsterminus: „polluter-pays principle“.

items.q: „verbindliches Ziel“ — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: Standardkollokation: „binding target“.

items.q: „Treibhausgasemissionen“ — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: Terminus: „greenhouse-gas emissions“.

items.q: „Ausstieg“ (aus einem Abkommen) — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: Völkerrechtsterminus: „withdrawal“ (from a treaty); „secession“ = Abspaltung.

items.q: The envoy would rather the pledge ____ quietly rather than announced at the summit.
items.e: „would rather" mit Bezug auf Vergangenes verlangt das Past Perfect: „would rather the pledge had been abandoned". Ausgeschlossen sind: „was abandoned" (Präteritum, das nach „would rather" nur den Gegenwartsbezug ausdrückt); „has been abandoned" (Present Perfect steht nach „would rather" nicht); „would be abandoned" (kein zweites „would" im Nebensatz).

items.q: Neither of the two drafts ____ circulated before the meeting, as the rules require.
items.e: „Neither of" verlangt den Singular, „before the meeting" die Vorzeitigkeit: „had been circulated". Ausgeschlossen sind: „were" und „have been" (Plural nach „Neither of"); „has been" (Singular zwar richtig, aber das Present Perfect bindet an die Gegenwart statt an den vergangenen Bezugspunkt).

items.q: Success depends ____ credible enforcement.
items.e: „depend on“ — feste Rektion.

items.q: The target is commensurate ____ the scale of the crisis.
items.e: „commensurate with“ = angemessen zu.

items.q: There is little appetite ____ further cuts.
items.e: „appetite for“ — Nomen-Rektion.

items.q: If the treaty ____ collapse, momentum would be lost.
items.e: „If X were to do …" bezeichnet die hypothetische Zukunft, die „would be lost" verlangt. Ausgeschlossen sind: „had been to" (bedeutet „war irgendwo gewesen" und ergibt hier keinen Sinn); „would" (im Bedingungssatz nicht möglich); „had to" (bedeutet „musste" — eine Tatsache der Vergangenheit, keine Hypothese).

items.q: Had the fund been capitalised in 2020, dozens of projects ____ under way at this very moment.
items.e: Gemischter Konditional: irreale Bedingung in der Vergangenheit („Had the fund been capitalised in 2020"), Folge in der Gegenwart („at this very moment") — verlangt „would be". Ausgeschlossen sind: „would have been" (Folge in der Vergangenheit, unvereinbar mit „at this very moment"); „had been" (Past Perfect gehört in den Bedingungssatz); „will be" (Indikativ Futur, unvereinbar mit der irrealen Bedingung).

items.q: ____ the pledge fail, the coalition would fracture.
items.e: Invertierter Konditional Typ I.

items.q: Little ____ how quickly the consensus would fray.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach „Little“.

items.q: The accord demands that each party ____ its inventory annually.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „demand that“.

items.q: ____ it not for the chair's insistence, the session would have adjourned without a text.
items.e: „Were it not for …" ist die feste invertierte Form der irrealen Bedingung. Ausgeschlossen sind: „Was" (in dieser Inversion nicht möglich); „Should" (ergäbe „Should it not for" — „should" verlangt einen Infinitiv, keine Präpositionalphrase); „Being" (Partizip ohne Satzfunktion).

items.q: The states risk ____ the target altogether.
items.e: „risk“ + Gerundium.

items.q: She remembered ____ the annex before the vote.
items.e: „remember doing“ = Erinnerung an Getanes.

items.q: Emissions ____ to have peaked in 2024.
items.e: Berichtspassiv: „are believed to have peaked“.

items.q: The fund is empty; the money ____ have been spent.
items.e: Epistemisches „must have been“.

items.q: There were six pledges, none of ____ was funded.
items.e: „none of which“ — relativer Anschluss.

items.q: ____ adequately financed, the plan could succeed.
items.e: Invertierter Konditional II.

items.q: This is the hottest year the planet ____ on record.
items.e: „the hottest … (that)“ + Present Perfect.

items.q: By the next COP, temperatures ____ the threshold.
items.e: „by the next COP“ + Future Perfect.

items.q: Neither of the two withdrawals ____ weakened the accord in practice.
items.e: „neither of …" bezeichnet keines von zweien und steht im formalen Register im Singular: „neither … has weakened". Ausgeschlossen sind: „have" (Plural, im Prüfungsregister nicht zulässig); „are" und „were" (Formen von „be" vor einem Vollverb-Partizip, das mit „have" gebildet wird).

items.q: So fragile ____ that a single exit imperilled it.
items.e: Inversion nach „So + Adjektiv“.

items.q: The new target is ____ stringent than the last.
items.e: Komparativ: „no less stringent than“.

items.q: ____ its imperfections, the accord endures.
items.e: „For all its imperfections“ = trotz.

items.q: It was the financing, ____ the ambition, that fell short.
items.e: Kontrast in der Cleft: „not the ambition“.

items.q: The bloc refuses to do ____ with the review mechanism.
items.e: „do away with“ = abschaffen.

items.q: The audit asked why the funds ____ disbursed.
items.e: Indirekte Frage, Vorzeitigkeit: Past Perfect Passiv.

items.q: What is the author's central contention regarding the Court's authority?
o: The Rome Statute enjoys universal acceptance among all states, including the permanent members.
The Court's authority is constrained by its dependence on contested jurisdiction and on state cooperation.
Territorial jurisdiction has been abandoned by the Court in favour of nationality-based jurisdiction.
Arrest warrants against sitting heads of state are always executed by the states parties concerned.
items.e: Kernthese im ersten Absatz: „the Court's writ runs only as far as states allow it to“ — die Autorität hängt von Zustimmung und Kooperation ab, die nicht alle Staaten leisten.
items.passage:
The International Criminal Court was conceived, in the optimistic afterglow of Rome in 1998, as the capstone of a slowly cohering system of international justice — the tribunal to which no perpetrator of the gravest crimes would ultimately be beyond reach. A quarter of a century on, that ambition sits awkwardly beside a starker reality: the Court's writ runs only as far as states allow it to, and jurisdiction, far from being a settled foundation, has become the terrain on which its legitimacy is fought over case by case.

The difficulty is structural rather than incidental. The Rome Statute binds only its parties, yet the Court has repeatedly asserted authority over nationals of non-member states where the alleged conduct occurred on the territory of a member, a reading that Washington, Moscow and Beijing alike have denounced as an unwarranted extension of treaty law to those who never consented to it. Prosecutors counter that territorial competence has always attached to the place of the crime, not the nationality of the accused, and that any other rule would let non-parties export impunity across their borders simply by dispatching nationals to commit it. Both positions are coherent; neither commands universal assent, and that absence of assent is precisely the point.

Arrest warrants issued against sitting heads of state have sharpened the quarrel further. States parties owe a treaty obligation to execute them, yet several have declined to do so when the wanted official arrived on a diplomatic visit, pleading competing obligations under customary immunity or simple political prudence. The Court has no marshals of its own; it depends entirely on the goodwill of governments it cannot compel, and each unexecuted warrant erodes the presumption that its rulings carry consequence rather than merely rhetorical weight.

None of this renders the institution ornamental. Even an unenforced warrant narrows a fugitive's travel, and the mere existence of a permanent forum has altered the calculations of some belligerents. But an institution whose authority rests on voluntary compliance is, by definition, only ever as strong as the least cooperative of its members choose to make it — a truth the Court's founders acknowledged in private, whatever they proclaimed in Rome.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, on what basis does the Court assert authority over nationals of non-member states?
o: Because the UN Security Council has referred every such case.
Because those states have signed a bilateral agreement with the Court.
Because customary international law binds all states regardless of consent.
Because the alleged conduct occurred on the territory of a member state.
items.e: Textbeleg: „the Court has repeatedly asserted authority over nationals of non-member states where the alleged conduct occurred on the territory of a member.“

States parties owe a treaty obligation to execute them, yet several have declined to do so when the wanted official arrived on a diplomatic visit, pleading competing obligations under customary immunity or simple political prudence. The Court has no marshals of its own; it depends entirely on the goodwill of governments it cannot compel, and each unexecuted warrant erodes the presumption that its rulings carry consequence rather than merely rhetorical weight.

None of this renders the institution ornamental. Even an unenforced warrant narrows a fugitive's travel, and the mere existence of a permanent forum has altered the calculations of some belligerents. But an institution whose authority rests on voluntary compliance is, by definition, only ever as strong as the least cooperative of its members choose to make it — a truth the Court's founders acknowledged in private, whatever they proclaimed in Rome.

items.q: Why do prosecutors defend the Court's approach to territorial jurisdiction?
o: Because nationality-based jurisdiction is far easier to prove in court.
Because the Charter of the United Nations expressly requires them to.
Because jurisdiction has always attached to the place where the crime occurred.
Because the non-member states have already consented to it informally.
items.e: Textbeleg: „territorial competence has always attached to the place of the crime, not the nationality of the accused.“
items.passage:
The International Criminal Court was conceived, in the optimistic afterglow of Rome in 1998, as the capstone of a slowly cohering system of international justice — the tribunal to which no perpetrator of the gravest crimes would ultimately be beyond reach. A quarter of a century on, that ambition sits awkwardly beside a starker reality: the Court's writ runs only as far as states allow it to, and jurisdiction, far from being a settled foundation, has become the terrain on which its legitimacy is fought over case by case.

The difficulty is structural rather than incidental. The Rome Statute binds only its parties, yet the Court has repeatedly asserted authority over nationals of non-member states where the alleged conduct occurred on the territory of a member, a reading that Washington, Moscow and Beijing alike have denounced as an unwarranted extension of treaty law to those who never consented to it. Prosecutors counter that territorial competence has always attached to the place of the crime, not the nationality of the accused, and that any other rule would let non-parties export impunity across their borders simply by dispatching nationals to commit it. Both positions are coherent; neither commands universal assent, and that absence of assent is precisely the point.

Arrest warrants issued against sitting heads of state have sharpened the quarrel further. States parties owe a treaty obligation to execute them, yet several have declined to do so when the wanted official arrived on a diplomatic visit, pleading competing obligations under customary immunity or simple political prudence. The Court has no marshals of its own; it depends entirely on the goodwill of governments it cannot compel, and each unexecuted warrant erodes the presumption that its rulings carry consequence rather than merely rhetorical weight.

None of this renders the institution ornamental. Even an unenforced warrant narrows a fugitive's travel, and the mere existence of a permanent forum has altered the calculations of some belligerents. But an institution whose authority rests on voluntary compliance is, by definition, only ever as strong as the least cooperative of its members choose to make it — a truth the Court's founders acknowledged in private, whatever they proclaimed in Rome.

items.q: The prosecutor decided to ____ the former minister on three counts of crimes against humanity.
items.e: „to indict“ = förmlich anklagen. „impeach“ betrifft Amtsenthebungsverfahren, „implicate“ = verwickeln ohne formale Anklage.

items.q: The court unsealed the ____ only after the suspect had been taken into custody.
items.e: „to unseal an indictment“ ist eine feste US-rechtliche Kollokation; eine bloße „allegation“ wird nicht „versiegelt“.

items.q: The suspect will be ____ before a judge within 48 hours of arrest.
items.e: „to arraign“ = dem Haftrichter vorführen und die Anklage verlesen; zeitlich vor jeder Verurteilung.

items.q: At the ____, the defendant entered a plea of not guilty.
items.e: Beim „arraignment“ (Vorführungstermin) wird das Plädoyer abgegeben, nicht bei der bloßen „indictment“ (Anklageschrift).

items.q: Facing overwhelming evidence, the defendant accepted a plea ____ rather than risk trial.
items.e: Feste Kollokation „plea bargain“; „deal“ ist umgangssprachlich und keine Fachkollokation, „pact/accord“ passen nicht.

items.q: The jury chose to ____ the defendant on all charges.
items.e: „to acquit somebody on a charge“ ist die feste strafprozessuale Kollokation; „exonerate/absolve“ nehmen kein „on“-Objekt in dieser Form.

items.q: The ____ was met with outrage among victims' families.
items.e: „acquittal“ = Freispruch nach Verhandlung; „dismissal“ wäre eine Abweisung schon vor der Verhandlung.

items.q: It took the jury only two hours to ____ him of fraud.
items.e: „to convict somebody of“ = für schuldig befinden; „sentence“ folgt erst nach der Verurteilung.

items.q: His earlier ____ was overturned on appeal after new evidence emerged.
items.e: „conviction“ = das Schuldurteil selbst, das im Berufungsverfahren aufgehoben werden kann.

items.q: The suspect remains in ____ pending trial.
items.e: „to remain in custody“ ist die feste Fügung für Untersuchungshaft; „arrest“ bezeichnet den Akt der Festnahme selbst.

items.q: Police were authorised to ____ the diplomat's driver for questioning.
items.e: „to detain somebody for questioning" ist die feste Wendung für die vorläufige Festhaltung zur Befragung — ohne förmliche Festnahme. Ausgeschlossen sind: „deter" (abschrecken, von einer Handlung abhalten); „deport" (außer Landes bringen — das schlösse die Befragung gerade aus); „depose" (ein Amt entziehen bzw. eine eidliche Aussage aufnehmen, die kein Festhalten voraussetzt).

items.q: The judge issued an arrest ____ naming the fugitive minister.
items.e: „arrest warrant“ = Haftbefehl; eine „summons“ lädt lediglich vor Gericht, ohne Festnahme anzuordnen.

items.q: He received a ____ ordering him to appear in court as a defendant.
items.e: „summons“ lädt eine Verfahrenspartei vor Gericht; „subpoena“ betrifft spezifisch Zeugen oder die Vorlage von Unterlagen.

items.q: The appellate court moved to ____ the indictment for lack of evidence.
items.e: „to quash an indictment" ist die feste Wendung des britischen Strafverfahrensrechts für die Aufhebung einer Anklage. Ausgeschlossen sind: „repeal" (bezieht sich ausschließlich auf Gesetze, nie auf Einzelakte); „revoke" (gilt für Erlaubnisse, Lizenzen und Vollmachten); „waive" (bedeutet den Verzicht auf ein eigenes Recht, nicht die Aufhebung einer Anklage).

items.q: On appeal, the higher court decided to ____ the jury's verdict.
items.e: „to overturn a verdict" ist die feste Wendung für die Aufhebung eines Urteilsspruchs durch die höhere Instanz. Ausgeschlossen sind: „repeal" (nur bei Gesetzen); „waive" (Verzicht auf ein eigenes Recht); „adjourn" (bedeutet die Vertagung einer Sitzung, nicht die Aufhebung einer Entscheidung).

items.q: The Supreme Court chose to ____ the lower court's decision in full.
items.e: „to uphold a decision“ = bestätigen; das Gegenteil von „overturn“.

items.q: The Home Secretary agreed to ____ the sentence in light of the prisoner's age and ill health.
items.e: „to commute a sentence" heißt, eine Strafe in eine mildere umzuwandeln — die feste Wendung für genau diesen Vorgang. Ausgeschlossen sind: „repeal" (nur bei Gesetzen); „waive" (Verzicht auf ein eigenes Recht, nicht Umwandlung einer Strafe); „adjourn" (Vertagung einer Sitzung).

items.q: The judge ordered the defendant ____ in custody until trial.
items.e: „to remand somebody in custody“ ist der feste strafprozessuale Ausdruck; die anderen Verben passen nicht in diese exakte Fügung.

items.q: Three judges sat on the ____ for the appeal, while the defendant watched from the dock.
items.e: „the bench“ bezeichnet die Richterbank bzw. die Richter kollektiv; „the dock“ ist der Platz des Angeklagten.

items.q: The case was added to the court's crowded ____ for next term.
items.e: „docket“ (v. a. AE) = Terminkalender bzw. Liste anhängiger Fälle.

items.q: ____ persons before the Court retain the right to a fair and public hearing.
items.e: „accused persons" ist der Verfahrensbegriff für die Beschuldigten, denen die Verfahrensgarantien zustehen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „Acquitted" und „Absolved" (beide bezeichnen den bereits Freigesprochenen — für ihn ist das Verfahren beendet); „Adjourned" (vertagt — das gilt für Sitzungen, nicht für Personen).

items.q: In domestic criminal trials, the ____ enjoys the presumption of innocence, just as the accused does before the Court.
items.e: „defendant“ ist das nationale Pendant zu „the accused“ vor dem IStGH; „claimant/plaintiff“ gehören zum Zivilprozess.

items.q: The panel was convened to ____ disputes over admissibility.
items.e: „to adjudicate a dispute" heißt, als entscheidende Instanz über ihn zu befinden — die Rolle eines eigens einberufenen Spruchkörpers. Ausgeschlossen sind: „litigate" (prozessieren — das tun die Parteien, nicht der Spruchkörper); „prosecute" (strafrechtlich verfolgen, Sache der Anklagebehörde); „legislate" (Gesetze erlassen, Sache des Gesetzgebers).

items.q: The doctrine under which a superior answers for crimes committed by subordinates he failed to prevent is known as command ____.
items.e: Der völkerstrafrechtliche Terminus lautet „command responsibility" — so in den Statuten der Ad-hoc-Tribunale und im Römischen Statut. Ausgeschlossen sind: „liability" (die zivilrechtliche Einstandspflicht; „command liability" ist kein Terminus); „accountability" (die allgemeine Rechenschaftspflicht); „culpability" (der Grad des Verschuldens im Einzelfall).

items.q: The victims' representatives were granted ____ to participate in the proceedings.
items.e: „to be granted standing“ = Klage-/Verfahrensbefugnis erhalten; „stance/stand“ sind klanglich nahe, aber falsche Distraktoren.

items.q: The registrar issued a ____ compelling the archivist to hand over the sealed correspondence.
items.e: „subpoena“ = gerichtliche Anordnung zur Vorlage von Unterlagen oder zum Erscheinen als Zeuge; „summons“ lädt lediglich eine Verfahrenspartei vor.

items.q: The prosecutor insisted that the witness ____ under oath.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „insist that“ — Grundform ohne -s.

items.q: It is essential that the accused ____ present at every hearing.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „it is essential that“ — bloße Grundform „be“.

items.q: Had the state ratified the Statute earlier, the Court ____ jurisdiction from the outset.
items.e: Typ-3-Konditional: die Inversion „Had the state ratified" ersetzt „If the state had ratified", und „from the outset" verankert die Folge in der Vergangenheit — verlangt ist „would have had". Ausgeschlossen sind: „had" (Past Perfect gehört in den Bedingungssatz, nicht in die Folge); „would" (ergibt „would jurisdiction", das Vollverb fehlt); „will have" (Indikativ Futur II, unvereinbar mit der irrealen Bedingung).

items.q: If the warrant ____ issued last year, the suspect would already be in custody today.
items.e: Gemischter Konditionalsatz: Bedingung in der Vergangenheit, Folge in der Gegenwart („today“).

items.q: ____ the delegation to walk out, the negotiations would collapse entirely.
items.e: Konditional-Inversion: „Were the delegation to walk out …“ = „If the delegation were to walk out …“. „Should“ verlangt den bloßen Infinitiv ohne „to“ und passt hier nicht.

items.q: ____ the panel to dismiss every charge at the confirmation stage, years of investigation would count for nothing.
items.e: „Were… to dismiss“ = hypothetische, konditionale Inversion mit „to“-Infinitiv.

items.q: Little ____ that the arrest warrant would provoke such a diplomatic backlash.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Little“: Hilfsverb vor Subjekt.

items.q: Under no circumstances ____ the identity of a protected witness be disclosed to the press.
items.e: Nach vorangestelltem „Under no circumstances" folgt die Inversion; vor dem Passiv-Infinitiv „be disclosed" kann nur ein Modalverb stehen: „may … be disclosed". Ausgeschlossen sind: „does" (nach „do" steht der reine Infinitiv, „does … be disclosed" ist ungrammatisch); „is" (ergäbe „is … be disclosed", zwei Formen von „be" nebeneinander); „has" (verlangte das Partizip „been").

items.q: He told the investigators that he ____ never met the accused before that night.
items.e: Past Perfect nach Backshift in der indirekten Rede (Vorzeitigkeit zum Berichtszeitpunkt).

items.q: She said the hearing ____ take place the following week, not that week.
items.e: Backshift von „will“ zu „would“ in der indirekten Rede; „the following week“ statt „next week“ (Deixisverschiebung).

items.q: They ____ have received the summons; the registry never sent it.
items.e: „can't have + Partizip II" bezeichnet den logischen Ausschluss: eine nie versandte Ladung kann niemand erhalten haben. Ausgeschlossen sind: „shouldn't have" (Vorwurf, der den Empfang voraussetzt); „needn't have" (unnötig, aber geschehen); „mustn't" (Verbot statt Schlussfolgerung).

items.q: The commander ____ have known about the massacre, given the volume of intercepted communications.
items.e: „must have“ = logische Gewissheit im Rückblick, gestützt durch den Beleg im Nebensatz.

items.q: ____ struck the observers most was the tribunal's restraint in sentencing.
items.e: Pseudo-Cleft-Satz: „What … was …“.

items.q: It was the absence of enforcement, not the absence of evidence, ____ ultimately doomed the case.
items.e: Im It-Cleft steht nach dem hervorgehobenen Satzglied das Relativum „that" — die im Prüfungsregister feste Wahl bei sachlichem Fokus. Ausgeschlossen sind: „whose" (Genitivrelativum, das ein folgendes Substantiv verlangt); „what" (leitet einen freien Relativsatz ein und kann nicht auf ein bereits genanntes Satzglied zurückweisen); „who" (bezieht sich nur auf Personen, nicht auf „the absence of enforcement").

items.q: The longer the warrant went unexecuted, ____ the Court's credibility appeared.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“; der zweite bestimmte Artikel ist obligatorisch.

items.q: The more governments ignore the warrants, ____ the deterrent effect becomes.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“ mit Komparativ im zweiten Satzglied.

items.q: No sooner had the warrant been issued ____ the minister cancelled his foreign trip.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „no sooner … than“; „then“ ist Adverb, kein Konnektor.

items.q: Hardly had the trial begun ____ the defence challenged the tribunal's jurisdiction.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „hardly … when“; nach vorangestelltem „Hardly“ steht die Inversion, danach „when“.

items.q: The ambassador is said ____ the memo days before the scandal broke.
items.e: Berichtspassiv mit Vorzeitigkeit: „is said to have drafted“.

items.q: The former general is widely believed ____ the massacre from a nearby command post.
items.e: Berichtspassiv „is believed to have ordered“ drückt Vorzeitigkeit zum jetzigen Glauben aus.

items.q: ____ before the tribunal in 2019, the general has never again left his home country.
items.e: Passivisches Partizip: der General wurde angeklagt, er klagte nicht selbst an.

items.q: ____ its jurisdictional limits, the Court has still secured a number of convictions.
items.e: „notwithstanding" ist die einzige der vier Formen, die als Präposition unmittelbar eine Nominalphrase regieren kann. Ausgeschlossen sind: „Although" und „Whereas" (Konjunktionen, die einen vollständigen Nebensatz mit finitem Verb verlangen — „Although its limits are …"); „However" (Adverb, das einen eigenen Hauptsatz einleitet und durch Komma abgetrennt wird).

items.q: He read the ruling and ____ at once.
items.e: Im britischen Recht- und Prüfungsregister ist „to appeal against a ruling" die feste Rektion. Ausgeschlossen sind: „appealed for it" („appeal for" heißt, etwas Erwünschtes zu erbitten — man erbittet kein Urteil, gegen das man vorgeht); „appealed to it" („appeal to" richtet sich an eine Person oder Instanz, nicht an die angefochtene Entscheidung); „it appealed" (verkehrt die Bedeutung ins „es gefiel ihm" und lässt den Bezug zum Urteil offen).

items.q: The prosecutor read the file and ____ its main findings before the hearing.
items.e: „to summarise something" ist transitiv und nimmt das Objekt ohne Präposition. Ausgeschlossen sind: „commented" (verlangt „on": „commented on its findings"); „remarked" (verlangt „on" bzw. „upon"); „alluded" (verlangt „to").

items.q: A number of witnesses ____ still to be interviewed by investigators.
items.e: „a number of“ + Plural — im Gegensatz zu „the number of“ + Singular.

items.q: The tribunal has yet to rule ____ the admissibility of the intercepted communications.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „rule on“ = entscheiden über; „rule over“ = herrschen über.

items.q: Which statement best captures the author's overall argument?
o: Bondholders now enjoy no legal remedies whatsoever against defaulting states abroad.
The shift from absolute to restrictive immunity has produced a single, uniform global standard.
The line between sovereign and commercial acts is still drawn differently in each forum.
Sovereign immunity has been abolished entirely in London, New York and Luxembourg alike.
items.e: Kernthese im ersten Absatz: „the line between the two continues to be drawn differently in London, New York and Luxembourg, with predictably untidy results.“
items.passage:
Few doctrines of international law have proved as resistant to tidy codification as sovereign immunity, and few have generated as much recent litigation. The old absolute rule — that a state and its property were simply beyond the reach of a foreign court — has given way almost everywhere to a restrictive doctrine distinguishing sovereign acts from commercial ones, yet the line between the two continues to be drawn differently in London, New York and Luxembourg, with predictably untidy results for litigants who find themselves arguing the same facts before three benches at once.

Nowhere has the doctrine been tested more severely than in suits brought by bondholders against defaulting governments. A state that issues debt in New York under New York law has, courts have increasingly held, surrendered its protection for that transaction even where the underlying purpose of the borrowing was unmistakably sovereign; the commercial character of the instrument, not the use to which the proceeds were put, now governs the inquiry. Creditors have pressed the logic further still, seeking to attach embassy bank accounts and even satellites, only to run into a separate and more stubborn wall: protection from execution survives even where protection from suit has fallen, and courts have generally refused to treat the two as interchangeable.

The resulting asymmetry frustrates claimants and defendants in roughly equal measure. A plaintiff may win a resounding judgment and then discover that almost nothing the defendant state owns abroad is actually attachable, since diplomatic and central-bank assets enjoy a separate, more robust layer of protection that survives even a clear commercial waiver. Governments, for their part, complain that the erosion of absolute immunity has turned ordinary sovereign borrowing into a minefield of foreign litigation, discouraging exactly the market access that developing states most need. Neither side has much cause for satisfaction, and the doctrine, restrictive in name, remains anything but restrained in the courtroom disputes it continues to generate.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, what determines whether a state's bond issuance counts as a commercial act?
o: The sovereign purpose for which the borrowed funds were ultimately put to use.
Whether the bond was issued before or after the state joined the United Nations.
The commercial character of the instrument, not the purpose of the borrowing.
The nationality of the majority of the bondholders bringing the claim.
items.e: Textbeleg: „the commercial character of the instrument, not the use to which the proceeds were put, now governs the inquiry.“

o: They routinely succeed, since any waiver of immunity from suit automatically extends to execution.
They run into a separate layer of protection that survives the loss of immunity from suit.

They succeed only in Luxembourg, and never in either London or New York.

o: The plaintiff must first obtain permission from the state's own courts before enforcing abroad.
The plaintiff automatically forfeits the judgment if the state pleads sovereign immunity.
The plaintiff can be certain of recovering the full amount from any state asset abroad.
The plaintiff may find that diplomatic and central-bank assets remain shielded from execution.

items.q: In the final paragraph, the word 'minefield' is used to convey that sovereign borrowing has become …

A state that issues debt in New York under New York law has, courts have increasingly held, surrendered its protection for that transaction even where the underlying purpose of the borrowing was unmistakably sovereign; the commercial character of the instrument, not the use to which the proceeds were put, now governs the inquiry. Creditors have pressed the logic further still, seeking to attach embassy bank accounts and even satellites, only to run into a separate and more stubborn wall: protection from execution survives even where protection from suit has fallen, and courts have generally refused to treat the two as interchangeable.

The resulting asymmetry frustrates claimants and defendants in roughly equal measure. A plaintiff may win a resounding judgment and then discover that almost nothing the defendant state owns abroad is actually attachable, since diplomatic and central-bank assets enjoy a separate, more robust layer of protection that survives even a clear commercial waiver. Governments, for their part, complain that the erosion of absolute immunity has turned ordinary sovereign borrowing into a minefield of foreign litigation, discouraging exactly the market access that developing states most need. Neither side has much cause for satisfaction, and the doctrine, restrictive in name, remains anything but restrained in the courtroom disputes it continues to generate.

items.q: What role does the final paragraph play in the overall argument?
o: To show that the asymmetry leaves both sides equally dissatisfied.
To argue that governments should return to the old absolute immunity rule.
To summarise the drafting history of the Rome Statute of the ICC.
To introduce a wholly new legal doctrine unrelated to state immunity.
items.e: Der Absatz erklärt, warum „Neither side has much cause for satisfaction“ — die Asymmetrie trifft Kläger wie beklagte Staaten gleichermaßen.

items.q: The bank sought to ____ the embassy's frozen account to satisfy the outstanding judgment.
items.e: „to attach an account“ ist die feste vollstreckungsrechtliche Kollokation; „seize/confiscate“ passen eher zu physischen Gütern im Strafrecht.

items.q: The court granted an order of ____ against the debtor's foreign-held assets.
items.e: „order of attachment“ ist der zivilprozessuale Fachterminus für die Sicherung von Vermögenswerten.

items.q: The bondholders sought to ____ the judgment against assets located in three separate jurisdictions.
items.e: „to enforce a judgment“ ist die Standardkollokation; „execute“ passt eher zu „a sentence“ oder „a warrant“.

items.q: The state's ____ on its sovereign bonds triggered a wave of litigation in three financial centres.
items.e: „default on a bond“ ist die feste finanzrechtliche Kollokation für Zahlungsausfall.

items.q: Foreign ____ filed suit in New York after the government missed its coupon payment.
items.e: „creditors" sind die Gläubiger, denen die ausgefallene Kuponzahlung zusteht — nur sie können daraus klagen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „curators" (Kuratoren einer Sammlung); „custodians" (Verwahrer fremder Wertpapiere, die im eigenen Namen nicht klagen); „contractors" (Auftragnehmer, die keine Anleihe halten).

items.q: The government argued that issuing the bonds was an act of ____ authority, not a commercial transaction.
items.e: „sovereign authority“ steht im Gegensatz zu „commercial transaction“ — die zentrale Unterscheidung der restriktiven Immunitätsdoktrin.

items.q: The claimant's lawyers argued the transaction was purely ____ in nature and therefore not shielded by immunity.
items.e: „commercial in nature“ ist die feste Fügung, die den Ausnahmetatbestand von der Immunität auslöst.

items.q: Central-bank reserves held abroad typically enjoy a separate layer of ____ from execution.
items.e: „protection from execution“ ist die feste vollstreckungsrechtliche Formel im Text.

items.q: The state formally ____ its immunity from suit when it agreed to New York law arbitration.
items.e: „to waive immunity" ist die feste Wendung für den Verzicht auf ein eigenes Recht. Ausgeschlossen sind: „repealed" (Gesetze aufheben — nie ein Recht im Einzelfall); „quashed" (eine Anklage oder Entscheidung aufheben, Sache eines Gerichts); „adjourned" (eine Sitzung vertagen).

items.q: The bank's counsel argued that the ____ did not extend automatically from immunity from suit to immunity from execution.
items.e: „waiver“ ist das feste Substantiv zu „waive“; die übrigen Optionen passen semantisch nicht zum rechtlichen Verzicht auf Immunität.

items.q: The tribunal was asked to rule on the state's plea of ____ immunity from prosecution before the civil courts.
items.e: „absolute immunity“ ist die ältere, umfassendere Doktrin, gegen die sich die restriktive Lehre im Text abgrenzt.

items.q: Courts have moved away from the doctrine under which no suit against a foreign state was ever ____ .
items.e: Nach „was" steht im Passiv das Partizip II: „was permitted". Ausgeschlossen sind: „permitting" (Partizip Präsens, das ein aktives Verhältnis ausdrückte); „permission" (Substantiv, das nach „was ever" kein Prädikat bildet); „permit" (Grundform bzw. Substantiv, in beiden Lesarten hier unmöglich).

items.q: The plaintiff obtained a favourable ____ but struggled for years to collect on it.
items.e: „to obtain a judgment“ und „to collect on a judgment“ sind die festen zivilprozessualen Fügungen; „verdict“ betrifft Jury-Entscheidungen im Strafrecht.

items.q: The government's assets abroad proved almost entirely ____ from attachment, frustrating the bondholders.
items.e: „immune from attachment" ist die vollstreckungsrechtliche Fügung: die Vermögenswerte sind dem Zugriff entzogen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „impervious" (undurchdringlich — verlangt „to", nicht „from"); „impregnable" (uneinnehmbar, von Festungen und Stellungen); „impassive" (regungslos, nur von Personen).

items.q: The dispute centred on whether the bond transaction fell within the commercial ____ to immunity.
items.e: „the commercial exception (to immunity)“ ist der stehende Fachbegriff für die Ausnahme bei kommerziellen Geschäften.

items.q: The court held that issuing debt under New York law amounted to a valid waiver of immunity ____ that transaction.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „a waiver for/covering a transaction“ — hier verlangt der Kontext „for“, nicht „of“.

items.q: The defaulting state's legal ____ deepened as more bondholders filed parallel suits abroad.
items.e: „legal exposure" ist das Maß der rechtlichen Angriffsfläche — der Fachausdruck für das Risiko, in Anspruch genommen zu werden. Ausgeschlossen sind: „exposition" (Darlegung eines Sachverhalts bzw. Ausstellung); „expiry" (Ablauf einer Frist); „expenditure" (Ausgaben).

items.q: The claimants sought to ____ a portion of the state's commercial revenue held in a New York account.
items.e: „to garnish“ = Forderungen gegenüber Dritten pfänden; die einschlägige Vollstreckungstechnik gegenüber Bankguthaben.

items.q: The central bank entered a formal ____ of sovereign immunity to resist the freezing order.
items.e: „to enter a plea of immunity“ ist die feste prozessuale Fügung; „plight“ ist ein Homophon-nahes Substantiv ohne juristische Bedeutung hier.

items.q: Restrictive immunity applies a ____ test to distinguish sovereign from commercial conduct.
items.e: „functional test“ ist der Fachbegriff für die Prüfung der Art der Handlung statt ihres Zwecks.

items.q: The bondholders' claim was ultimately ____ by a New York court applying commercial-activity principles.
items.e: „to uphold a claim“ = einer Klage stattgeben; die übrigen Formen sind keine gebräuchlichen juristischen Verben.

items.q: The bank argued that central-bank ____ , unlike ordinary commercial deposits, could never be attached.
items.e: „central-bank reserves“ ist die im Text zentrale Fachkollokation für die besonders geschützten Vermögenswerte.

items.q: The tribunal found that the transaction, though initiated by the ministry, was ____ commercial.
items.e: Vor einem Adjektiv steht ein Adverb; „substantively" bezeichnet die Beurteilung nach dem Wesen der Sache. Ausgeschlossen sind: „substantiated" (belegt, bewiesen — Partizip, das kein Adjektiv modifizieren kann); „substantiating" (belegend — ebenfalls Partizip); „substantial" (Adjektiv, das vor einem weiteren Adjektiv nicht stehen kann).

items.q: The court's ____ jurisdiction over the dispute rested on the commercial-activity exception.
items.e: „subject-matter jurisdiction“ = sachliche Zuständigkeit, hier begründet über die kommerzielle Ausnahme.

items.q: Every ____ before the New York court had raised broadly the same commercial-activity argument.
items.e: „litigant“ = Verfahrenspartei; „litigator“ bezeichnet den Prozessanwalt, nicht die Partei selbst.

items.q: The only ____ still open to the bondholders was to pursue assets in a third jurisdiction.
items.e: „remedy" ist im Rechtsenglischen der Rechtsbehelf — die Möglichkeit, einen Anspruch durchzusetzen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „resource" (Mittel oder Vorrat, nicht Rechtsbehelf); „remittance" (Geldüberweisung); „remission" (Erlass einer Strafe oder Schuld — hier wird nichts erlassen, sondern verfolgt).

items.q: The court insisted that the state ____ full documentation of the transaction.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „insist that“ — Grundform ohne -s.

items.q: It is imperative that the ruling ____ published before the appeal deadline.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „it is imperative that“ — bloße Grundform „be“.

items.q: Had the bank filed the claim a year earlier, the assets ____ still frozen at trial.
items.e: Typ-3-Konditionalsatz: irreale Vergangenheitsbedingung, Folge ebenfalls in der Vergangenheit.

items.q: If the waiver ____ signed before the default, the creditors could have attached the reserves immediately.
items.e: Typ-3-Konditional: „had been signed“ als irreale Vorzeitigkeit; die Folge „could have attached“ bestätigt den Bezug zur Vergangenheit.

items.q: ____ the tribunal to rule against the state, enforcement would still prove elusive.
items.e: „Were … to rule“ = hypothetische, konditionale Inversion mit „to“-Infinitiv.

items.q: ____ the gold reserve ever leave the central bank's custody, the creditors' claim would collapse.
items.e: „Should" + Infinitiv ohne „to" leitet die unwahrscheinliche Bedingung ein und ist die einzige Form, die den unflektierten „leave" trägt. Ausgeschlossen sind: „If" (verlangt bei „the gold reserve" den Indikativ „leaves"); „Was" (Präteritum ohne Infinitivrektion); „Were" (verlangt „to leave").

items.q: Little ____ that the waiver would later be contested on execution grounds.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Little“: Hilfsverb vor Subjekt.

items.q: Under no circumstances ____ the reserves be treated as ordinary commercial funds.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Under no circumstances“: Hilfsverb vor Subjekt.

items.q: He told the court that the ministry ____ never authorised the transaction in question.
items.e: Past Perfect nach Backshift in der indirekten Rede (Vorzeitigkeit zum Berichtszeitpunkt).

items.q: The bank stated that the funds ____ be released the following month, not that month.
items.e: Backshift von „will“ zu „would“ in der indirekten Rede; „the following month“ statt „next month“ (Deixisverschiebung).

items.q: The registry ____ have misfiled the waiver; it simply cannot be located.
items.e: „must have“ = logische Gewissheit im Rückblick.

items.q: The bondholders ____ have known that central-bank reserves enjoy separate protection; their filings ignore the distinction entirely.
items.e: „can't have known“ = logische Unmöglichkeit im Rückblick, gestützt durch den nachfolgenden Beleg.

items.q: ____ frustrated the claimants most was the unattachability of the reserves.
items.e: Pseudo-Cleft-Satz: „What … was …“.

items.q: It was the commercial character of the bond, not its sovereign purpose, ____ ultimately governed the inquiry.
items.e: Das It-Cleft verlangt bei sachlichem Fokus das Relativum „that". Ausgeschlossen sind: „who" (nur bei Personen); „whose" (Genitivrelativum ohne folgendes Substantiv); „what" (freies Relativum ohne Rückbezug auf ein genanntes Satzglied).

items.q: The longer the litigation dragged on, ____ the bondholders' prospects of recovery appeared.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“; der zweite bestimmte Artikel ist obligatorisch.

items.q: The more assets a claimant identifies abroad, ____ the chance of eventual recovery.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“ mit Komparativ im zweiten Satzglied.

items.q: No sooner had the judgment been entered ____ the bondholders moved to attach the account.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „no sooner … than“; „then“ ist Adverb, kein Konnektor.

items.q: Hardly had the reserves been identified ____ the central bank asserted its immunity.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „hardly … when“; nach vorangestelltem „Hardly“ steht die Inversion, danach „when“.

items.q: The bank is said ____ the funds weeks before the freezing order was granted.
items.e: Berichtspassiv mit Vorzeitigkeit: „is said to have moved“.

items.q: The ministry is widely believed ____ the waiver without realising its scope.
items.e: Berichtspassiv „is believed to have signed“ drückt Vorzeitigkeit zum jetzigen Glauben aus.

items.q: ____ under New York law, the bond lost its shield of sovereign immunity for that transaction.
items.e: Passivisches Partizip: die Anleihe wurde begeben, sie begab nicht selbst.

items.q: ____ the restrictive doctrine, several states still resist any narrowing of their immunity.
items.e: Nur „notwithstanding" kann als Präposition direkt vor einer Nominalphrase stehen. Ausgeschlossen sind: „Whereas" und „Although" (verlangen einen finiten Nebensatz); „However" (Adverb, das einen eigenständigen Hauptsatz einleitet).

items.q: She read the ruling and immediately ____ the Supreme Court for a stay of execution.
items.e: „to appeal to somebody for something" = sich mit einer Bitte an eine Instanz wenden; Adressat ist das Gericht, Gegenstand die Aussetzung. Ausgeschlossen sind: „appealed on" („appeal on" leitet nur den Rechtsgrund ein — „on procedural grounds" —, nie den Adressaten); „appealed at" (diese Rektion gibt es nicht); „appealed against" (richtet sich gegen die angefochtene Entscheidung, nicht an das Gericht, und passt nicht zum Anschluss „for a stay").

items.q: The clerk read the filing and ____ the discrepancy before the hearing began.
items.e: „to report something" ist transitiv und nimmt das Objekt unmittelbar. Ausgeschlossen sind: „objected" (verlangt „to"); „protested" (im britischen Gebrauch „protested against"); „complained" (verlangt „about" bzw. „of").

items.q: A number of claimants ____ still awaiting a ruling on admissibility.
items.e: „a number of“ + Plural — im Gegensatz zu „the number of“ + Singular.

items.q: The court has yet to rule ____ the immunity of the central bank's reserves.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „rule on“ = entscheiden über; „rule over“ = herrschen über.

items.q: What is the author's principal claim in this passage?
o: Reform of the mechanism was completed decades ago and no longer generates debate.
A once-uncontroversial mechanism has become contentious and is now being renegotiated.
The mechanism has remained an uncontroversial, technical arrangement throughout its history.
Host states have universally abandoned their investment treaties altogether.
items.e: Kernthese: „It has instead become one of the more contentious features of the treaty system... reform... is now the subject of active multilateral negotiation.“
items.passage:
For thirty years, investor-state dispute settlement was the quiet plumbing of the international economic order: a mechanism, embedded in thousands of treaties, allowing a foreign investor to sue a host government directly before an arbitral tribunal rather than trust to that government's own courts. It was meant to reassure capital that political risk would not go uncompensated. It has instead become one of the more contentious features of the treaty system it was designed to underpin, and reform, once a marginal concern of academic conferences, is now the subject of active multilateral negotiation.

The complaints are by now familiar, if not always fair. Arbitrators, critics note, are drawn from a small pool of practitioners who alternate between sitting as adjudicators and appearing as counsel, an arrangement that would raise eyebrows in any domestic judiciary but has long been tolerated in a system built by and for specialists. Awards have occasionally reached sums that dwarf the annual health budgets of the states ordered to pay them, and the mere threat of a claim, defenders of reform argue, has chilled legitimate regulatory measures on public health and the environment — a phenomenon dubbed regulatory chill, whose scale remains disputed but whose existence few now deny outright.

Two reform paths have gained real traction. One, favoured chiefly in Brussels, would replace ad hoc tribunals with a standing investment court staffed by tenured judges, answerable to an appellate body rather than to the parties who selected them. The other, preferred in Washington and several capitals wary of ceding sovereignty to a permanent bench, would leave the arbitral model largely intact while tightening the substantive standards investors may invoke and narrowing the discretion tribunals enjoy in awarding damages. Neither camp has persuaded the other, and a growing number of states have simply opted out of the system altogether, terminating older treaties rather than waiting for a reform that may never arrive. The result is not consensus but fragmentation — a patchwork in which some investors retain robust protection and others, increasingly, none at all.

One, favoured chiefly in Brussels, would replace ad hoc tribunals with a standing investment court staffed by tenured judges, answerable to an appellate body rather than to the parties who selected them. The other, preferred in Washington and several capitals wary of ceding sovereignty to a permanent bench, would leave the arbitral model largely intact while tightening the substantive standards investors may invoke and narrowing the discretion tribunals enjoy in awarding damages. Neither camp has persuaded the other, and a growing number of states have simply opted out of the system altogether, terminating older treaties rather than waiting for a reform that may never arrive. The result is not consensus but fragmentation — a patchwork in which some investors retain robust protection and others, increasingly, none at all.

items.q: In the phrase 'the quiet plumbing of the international economic order', 'plumbing' is used to suggest that ISDS was originally seen as …
o: a visible and much-celebrated centrepiece of economic diplomacy.
an unglamorous but functionally essential background mechanism.
a source of constant public controversy from its very inception.
a purely ornamental legal fiction of no practical use.
items.e: Metaphorisch: „plumbing“ bezeichnet unauffällige, aber notwendige Infrastruktur — passend zu „quiet“.
items.passage:
For thirty years, investor-state dispute settlement was the quiet plumbing of the international economic order: a mechanism, embedded in thousands of treaties, allowing a foreign investor to sue a host government directly before an arbitral tribunal rather than trust to that government's own courts. It was meant to reassure capital that political risk would not go uncompensated. It has instead become one of the more contentious features of the treaty system it was designed to underpin, and reform, once a marginal concern of academic conferences, is now the subject of active multilateral negotiation.

The complaints are by now familiar, if not always fair. Arbitrators, critics note, are drawn from a small pool of practitioners who alternate between sitting as adjudicators and appearing as counsel, an arrangement that would raise eyebrows in any domestic judiciary but has long been tolerated in a system built by and for specialists. Awards have occasionally reached sums that dwarf the annual health budgets of the states ordered to pay them, and the mere threat of a claim, defenders of reform argue, has chilled legitimate regulatory measures on public health and the environment — a phenomenon dubbed regulatory chill, whose scale remains disputed but whose existence few now deny outright.

The other, preferred in Washington and several capitals wary of ceding sovereignty to a permanent bench, would leave the arbitral model largely intact while tightening the substantive standards investors may invoke and narrowing the discretion tribunals enjoy in awarding damages. Neither camp has persuaded the other, and a growing number of states have simply opted out of the system altogether, terminating older treaties rather than waiting for a reform that may never arrive. The result is not consensus but fragmentation — a patchwork in which some investors retain robust protection and others, increasingly, none at all.

items.q: The author's tone in presenting the two reform camps is best described as …
o: balanced, presenting each camp's position without declaring a winner.
strongly partisan in favour of the standing investment court model.
openly mocking of both Brussels and Washington in equal measure.
dismissive of both proposals as fundamentally unworkable in law.
items.e: Beide Reformwege werden sachlich nebeneinandergestellt („Neither camp has persuaded the other“) — ausgewogener, nicht wertender Ton.
